Nephew
NEF-yoo
noun
From the Latin nepos, “grandson, descendant,” through the Old French neveu. In older English it means a grandson or a descendant generally; the restriction to a brother’s or sister’s son is a later development.

Biblical Definition

A nephew in the KJV is not a brother’s or sister’s son, as we now use the word, but a grandson — and more broadly a descendant, one of a man’s posterity. The word comes through the Latin nepos, grandson. So Paul charges the church that a widow’s “children or nephews” should “requite their parents” (1Ti 5:4) — her children and grandchildren, the generations she raised, are to care for her in age; piety begins at home and flows down the line and back up it. In judgment the word marks the cutting-off of a whole house: of the wicked it is said, “He shall neither have son nor nephew among his people” (Job 18:19), no child and no grandchild, his name blotted from the earth. So too against Babylon: “I will... cut off from Babylon the name, and remnant, and son, and nephew” (Isa 14:22) — root and branch, seed and seed’s seed. Set against these curses stands the covenant blessing, for “children’s children are the crown of old men” (Pro 17:6). The grandchild is no small thing in Scripture: he is the visible token of a covenant kept to a thousand generations. To read nephew as a sibling’s child is to lose the sweep of the promise — the AV means thy seed after thee, the posterity in whom God shews His faithfulness.

Webster 1828 Definition

A grandson, or a descendant generally — not a brother’s or sister’s son.

NEPHEW, a grandson; and by extension any descendant of the second generation or beyond.

From Latin nepos, “grandson,” through Old French neveu.

The modern restriction to a sibling’s son arose after the KJV was made.

A widow’s nephews are her grandchildren, bound to requite her (1Ti 5:4).

To have neither son nor nephew is to be cut off root and branch (Job 18:19).

Key Scripture

1Ti 5:4 — "But if any widow have children or nephews, let them learn first to shew piety at home, and to requite their parents: for that is good and acceptable before God."

Job 18:19 — "He shall neither have son nor nephew among his people, nor any remaining in his dwellings."

Isa 14:22 — "For I will rise up against them, saith the LORD of hosts, and cut off from Babylon the name, and remnant, and son, and nephew, saith the LORD."

Pro 17:6 — "Children's children are the crown of old men; and the glory of children are their fathers."

Modern Corruption

No redefinition, only a shift of kinship: the KJV’s nephew is a grandson, while ours is a sibling’s child.

expand to see more

The modern reader hears nephew and thinks of his brother’s or sister’s boy, and so misreads 1Ti 5:4 as a charge laid on the wider family rather than on the direct line of descent. But the AV means grandson: the widow’s own children’s children, raised in her house, are to requite her in her age. The confusion is easily cleared by the Latin root nepos, grandson, which the older English kept. Read it so, and the passage speaks its plain domestic duty: the generations a mother has poured herself into owe her honour and support when she is old, and to give it is good and acceptable before God.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the covenant reach of God’s dealings to a thousand generations — blessing and judgment alike running down the line of seed. To be left “neither son nor nephew” (Job 18:19) is the terror pronounced on the wicked: a name utterly cut off, no grandchild to carry it. To have one’s “son, and nephew” struck from Babylon (Isa 14:22) is judgment to the third generation. But the covenant turns the same reach to mercy: “children’s children are the crown of old men” (Pro 17:6). The grandchild is the visible proof of a promise kept — the LORD showing mercy unto thousands of them that love Him.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Nephew means a grandson or descendant, from Latin nepos — not a sibling’s child.

Nephew — from Latin nepos, “grandson,” via Old French neveu.

In the KJV it means a grandson, or a descendant more broadly.

The modern sense of a sibling’s son is a later narrowing.

A widow’s nephews are her grandchildren, bound to requite her (1Ti 5:4).

Children’s children are the covenant crown of old age (Pro 17:6).

Usage

"“If any widow have children or nephews” — the KJV means her grandchildren, not her nieces and nephews."

"Neither son nor nephew: no child and no grandchild left to keep the name alive."

"The nephew of Scripture is a man’s seed after him, the crown of his old age."
